newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice asks SEC, IRS to review yield burning.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice asks SEC, IRS to review yield burning.

text.p: U.S. Justice Department has asked the SEC and IRS to review possible yield burning by municipal bond firms and to advise the department whether it should sue any offenders under the 1986 Federal Claims Act, according to a Justice Department letter.

Frank Hunger, assistant attorney general for Justice, made the request in letters March 19 to William McLucas, enforcement chief of Securities and Exchange Commission, and Richard Calahan, deputy inspector general for Treasury.

Hunger was responding to a Feb 5 request by Sen. Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, that Justice and the Internal Revenue Service invoke the federal claims law to recover millions of dollars that the agencies and localities allegedly are owed by Wall Street due to yield burning.

The $1.3 trillion municipal bond market has been rocked by recent charges that bond underwriters overbill issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond financing transactions, a practice dubbed yield burning.

The 1986 federal claims law permits the federal government to take action against any party that brings financial loss to Treasury. Justice could seek treble damages and penalities against defendants in such cases.

The strategy would take the weight off muni bond issuers who are being urged by Treasury to IRS under a 1996 "revenue procedure" to pay off yield burning debts even though localities claim they had no knowledge of the practice.

"Sen. Grassley suggests that the Department of Justice consider suit against investment banking firms under the False Claims Act or other available remedies if any investigation concludes that overcharges occurred," Hunger's letter to regulators says.
"After you have an opportunity to review the matter, please advise us if you believe that any action by the Justice is appropriate," Hunger's letter to Calahan and McLucas adds.
Andrew Fois, another of Justice's assistant attorney generals, meanwhile, told Grassley in a March 25 letter that the department had contacted SEC and Treasury on the matter.

Fois' letter said it is "usual practice" for Justice to refer requests like Grassley's to the agencies with "investigative responsibility" for the areas - in this case SEC, which oversees investment banking firms, and the office of inspector general at Treasury.

Grassley also got a letter from IRS Commissioner Margaret Richardson, who said IRS and Treasury are reviewing comments they got in response to the yield burning "revenue procedure" it issued last year.
IRS officials signaled at recent public hearings on the controversial procedure that the Service may revise it.

"The IRS and Treasury Department are currently reviewing the written and oral comments received," Richardson said. "I appreciate your concern that the IRS and Treasury resolve the complex compliance issues in a manner that is best for both taxpayers and tax administration," Richardson said.
